units.text: Therefore, this study aimed to evaluate the effect of urban landscape structure on ant and spider communities. More specifically, we evaluated the hypothesis that (I) the landscape proportion of Atlantic Forest cover has a positive effect on the taxonomic and functional richness of spiders and ants; (II) the mean isolation of forest patches in the landscapes has a negative impact on the taxonomic and functional richness of spiders and ants; (III) the mean shape complexity of forest patches in the landscapes has a negative effect on taxonomic and functional richness due to deleterious edge effects on the biodiversity associated with the forest remnants; and (IV) the landscape structure has an effect on the ant and spider community compositions.

Because of the colonial behavior prevalent between ant species (Longino 2000), to build the ant community matrix, the incidence of the samples within each sampling unit was used instead of the total number of individuals collected whereas the spider community matrix was composed of the total abundance in each sampling unit (forest patch). The functional community structure was represented by the functional groups’ presence/absence matrix in each sampling unit for both ants and spiders. Both taxonomic and functional richness was calculated for ants and spiders. To analyze the variation in ant and spider community compositions, the dimensionality of the community matrices was reduced to a pair of synthetic axes using a nonmetric multi-dimensional scaling (NMDS) ordination technique with the Bray-Curtis index as a measure of dissimilarity. The analysis was performed separately for assemblages of ants and spiders, using the respective community matrices described above, where species abundance was normalized by the subtraction of the mean value and dividing by the standard deviation, which avoids problems with scale differences between the variations of different species. The final NMDSs can be considered great representations of both ant and spider communities, with the stress of 0.17 and 0.16, respectively (Supplementary Information Fig S1). The NMDSs were performed using the R software version 3.6.1, package Vegan, version 2.5-6 (Oksanen et al 2016).

Ant species richness was strongly negatively related to the landscape mean fractal dimension (β = − 0.77; Fig 2a). Regarding ant communities’ composition, variations represented by the synthetic variables NMDS1 and NMDS2 were also both strongly negatively related to the landscape mean fractal dimension (respectively β = − 0.88, β = − 0.7; Fig 2b and c; Supplementary Information Fig S7 a). There was no clear or apparent association between the ant NMDS1 and NMDS2, with no changes in the proportion of ant subfamilies nor functional groups (respectively Fig 3a and b; Supplementary Information Fig S7 b and c). However, the ant community composition variation, represented in the synthetic variable NMDS1, is associated with the species loss in the landscape mean fractal dimension (Fig 2), since NMDS1 is significantly related to ant species richness, to which at least 61% of NMDS1 variation can be attributed (β = 0.78, F 1 ,12 = 18.96, R 2 = 0.61, p
